idiom_name: transformation value = reducing function -> reducing function, applied by a driver that owns source, sink and completion
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define a reducing function as init() -> acc, step(acc, element) -> acc and complete(acc) -> result; define a transducer as a transformation of that triple and compose transducers with ordinary function composition, so a stack is itself a value rather than a process. Apply it with a driver that owns exactly the two things the transducer must not know: the input process (collection, cursor, channel, file, generator) and the output accumulator (vector, map, counter, string builder, writer) - plus the loop that stops as soon as a stage signals 'done'. Keep stages pure where possible; a stateful stage (take, dedupe, partition) must take its state from the driver so one pipeline value can be applied to many runs. Nothing is materialised between stages: the composed stack is called element by element and completion, early termination and any buffered tail flush flow through the same triple.
code_sketch:
step(acc, x) -> acc            # the 'job': supplied by the sink at application time
complete(acc) -> result        # arity-1 completion / flush of buffered stages
transducer = rf -> rf'         # a transformation of the reducing function
pipeline = compose(stages...)  # a value, not a process
result = driver(pipeline(step), complete, source)   # source and sink chosen here
pitfalls: Skipping the completion call loses the buffered tail of stateful stages and leaves take/drop unable to stop the source.
Creating a stateful stage's state at construction time (instead of per application) turns a reusable pipeline into a one-shot value.
Letting the driver capture the source inside the transducer re-couples the two contexts the pattern exists to separate.

Wrong move: applying an eduction or sequence over an infinite source and trusting take to stop reading -> the chunked-sequence conversion can pull whole 32-element batches, hanging or exhausting memory before take fires -> instead take from a finite source or use plain lazy sequence operations for infinite inputs.

Wrong move: reaching for transducers because you want concurrency or backpressure -> the transducer says nothing about threads, transports or buffering, so the pipeline still runs wherever the driver runs -> instead pair the stack with a driver that owns flow control (core.async pipeline/onto-chan, or a reactive/observable runtime).
